segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: This is how a person should regard us: as Christ's assistants and stewards of God's secrets.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now in this matter what is required of stewards is that one be found faithful.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But to me it is a very small thing that I should be examined by you or by any human court; in fact, I do not even examine myself.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For I am aware of nothing against myself, but I am not vindicated by that; the one who examines me is the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So do not judge anything before the time, until the Lord comes. He will bring to light the things hidden in darkness and make plain the intentions of hearts, and then each one's praise will come from God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now, brothers and sisters, I have applied these things to myself and Apollos for your sake, so that from us you may learn the saying “Not beyond what is written,” so that none of you is puffed up in favor of the one against the other.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For who marks you out as different? What do you have that you did not receive? And if you did receive it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Already you have had your fill! Already you have become rich! Without us you have become kings! And I wish you really had become kings, so that we too might be kings with you!

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For it seems to me that God has put us apostles on show last of all, like men condemned to death, because we have become a spectacle to the world, both to angels and to people.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: We are fools because of Christ, but you are sensible in Christ. We are weak, but you are strong. You are honored, but we are dishonored.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: To this very hour we go hungry and thirsty, we are poorly clothed, we are knocked about, we have no home,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and we toil, working with our own hands. When insulted, we bless; when persecuted, we endure;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: when slandered, we answer kindly. We have become like the scum of the world, the scrapings of everything, right up to now.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I am not writing these things to shame you, but to warn you as my beloved children.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For though you may have ten thousand guardians in Christ, you do not have many fathers; for in Christ Jesus, through the good news, it was I who fathered you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So I urge you: become imitators of me.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For this reason I have sent Timothy to you, who is my beloved and faithful child in the Lord. He will remind you of my ways in Christ Jesus, just as I teach everywhere in every assembly.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But some have become puffed up, as though I were not coming to you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But I will come to you soon, if the Lord wills, and I will find out not the talk of those who are puffed up but their power,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for the kingdom of God does not consist in talk but in power.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in love and a spirit of gentleness?

notes.note: The Greek word denotes a subordinate who carries out someone else's instructions: an aide, attendant or junior official. It is not Paul's usual word for a servant or a slave, and 'assistants' keeps that distinction visible. Most modern translations have 'servants'.

In the Greek Scriptures and in Paul the word means something God has kept hidden and now discloses, not a puzzle or something beyond understanding, which is what 'mystery' suggests today. Most translations keep 'mysteries', and some scholars defend it as an established technical term.

A steward was the manager of a household or estate, often himself a slave, who ran the owner's affairs and answered to the owner alone. That is the point of verses 2 to 5: a steward is assessed by his master, not by the rest of the household.

The Greek says literally 'a human day', meaning a day of judgment set by human beings. The phrase is coined to contrast with 'the Day' of the Lord's judgment mentioned in 3:13. English translations generally paraphrase it as a human court or human judgment.

The verb belongs to the word-family English splits between 'righteous' and 'just', and is traditionally rendered 'justify'. Here the setting is a judicial examination, and the meaning is to be declared in the right. Several modern versions accordingly have 'acquitted' or 'innocent' at this verse.

The verb normally means to change the form or appearance of something, and its exact sense here is debated. The usual view is that Paul has cast his argument in terms of himself and Apollos as an illustration, perhaps to avoid naming those in Corinth whom it really concerns. Others take it to mean simply that he has spoken figuratively, through the images of gardeners, builders and stewards.

The Greek is a terse phrase with no verb, introduced as if it were a known saying. Most interpreters take 'what is written' to mean Scripture, perhaps the passages Paul has quoted in chapters 1 to 3. Its origin and exact force are uncertain, and a few scholars have suspected that the text is damaged at this point.

The picture is drawn from public shows in the arena or theater, or possibly from a victory procession. Condemned prisoners were brought on at the end to be killed before the crowd. Paul pictures the apostles in that last place, with the whole universe as the audience.

This word and the one rendered 'scrapings' both refer to the dirt removed when something is scoured or wiped clean. Both were also used as insults for worthless people. Some scholars think they also allude to human scapegoats sacrificed to purify a city, which would make the apostles victims on behalf of others, but whether Paul intends that is disputed.

The word refers to the household slave who escorted a boy to school and supervised his conduct until he came of age. He was a minder and disciplinarian, not a teacher. The contrast is between any number of hired supervisors and the one father.

The Greek was an ordinary word for a public announcement of good news, including imperial proclamations. 'Gospel' has become a purely religious term or a book title. Many modern translations alternate between the two renderings.

A first-century hearer knew this word as a civic gathering of citizens and as the Greek Scriptures' term for Israel assembled. 'Church' now suggests a building or an institution. 'Church' is the near-universal rendering, and 'assembly' should be understood here as a standing community, not a single meeting.
'Meekness' now suggests weakness or timidity, which the Greek does not; the word describes someone who is not harsh or self-assertive. 'Gentleness' or 'humility' is the mainstream modern rendering.

candidates.reason: It recurs across the Gospels, Paul and Revelation; 'mystery' and 'secret' give the reader different impressions, and the choice should be uniform.
The plural address to mixed congregations occurs in nearly every letter, and translations vary between 'brothers', 'brothers and sisters' and 'friends'.
'Kingdom', 'reign' and 'rule' are all defensible, and the choice affects wordplay with βασιλεύω, as in verse 8 of this chapter.
It is used of temple officers, synagogue attendants and apostolic helpers, and needs a rendering distinct from διάκονος and δοῦλος so that readers do not see three Greek words as one 'servant'.
It is very frequent, with senses ranging from urge and appeal to comfort and encourage, so a rendering per sense should be fixed to keep chapters consistent.
